readerTitle: Would it still work if they could see what you did?
caseNote: 가상 사례 (빵집 간판, 사내 고객지원팀 인력 요청, 화물 운송 계약) · 원칙 출처는 Thaler & Sunstein의 Nudge
insight: 설득과 조작을 가르는 것은 기법이 아니라, 상대가 내가 한 일을 전부 알아도 여전히 통하느냐다.
misconception: 심리를 이용하면 모두 조작이다. 또는 합법이고 효과가 있으면 괜찮다.

sources.text: Thaler, R. & Sunstein, C. (2008). Nudge. Yale University Press. (Rawls의 publicity principle을 넛지 판단 기준으로 논의)

factChecks.note: Nudge(2008)가 Rawls의 publicity principle(공개해도 정당화할 수 있는가)을 기준으로 논의한다는 점을 원문에서 확인하세요. 카드 5에는 '책에서 다룬 생각'으로만 적었습니다.
빵집, 고객지원팀, 화물 운송 사례는 모두 가상입니다. 수치(응답 시간 등)는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two bakeries, the same sign.
body: Two bakery windows on the same street both say: *Only 3 loaves left today.*

One baker counted the shelf at 4 p.m. The other prints the sign every morning. The words are identical. The sales bump may be identical too. Only one of them would be embarrassed if you walked in and asked.

image.label: Two bakery windows with the same 'Only 3 left' sign
image.brief: 나란히 있는 빵집 창문 두 개에 똑같은 "Only 3 loaves left today" 손글씨 표지판. 왼쪽 창문 안은 선반이 거의 비어 있고, 오른쪽은 빵이 가득 쌓여 있음. 따뜻한 오후 햇빛. 실제 상호나 로고 없음.

cards.title: You need two more people on your team.
body: You run the customer support team at a mid-size company. The queue has been long for months, and you want your VP to approve two hires. You have one meeting.
How do you make the case?

options.text: Show the real backlog trend, what two hires would fix, and that it may ease a little in summer
options.feedback: You give up a bit of drama, but the VP decides on the true picture. If it's approved, your next request starts with credibility.

options.text: Show only your worst week, presented as a typical one
options.feedback: It may win the meeting. But it works only because the VP can't see the other weeks, and that lasts until the next report.

options.text: Open with one angry customer's email, then show the data
options.feedback: A vivid story helps people feel a real problem. It's fair if that email is typical, and misleading if it's the rare worst case.

cards.title: Both pitches can win. Only one survives.
body: Say you pick the worst-week deck and get the hires. Three months later, the normal numbers show up in the monthly report. They look nothing like your slides.
The VP doesn't reverse the decision. She just quietly discounts every forecast you bring from now on. The pitch worked once and cost you every pitch after it.

cards.title: Persuasion vs manipulation
body: **Persuasion** changes a decision by helping people see their situation more clearly: better evidence, a clearer story, the real costs and benefits.
**Manipulation** changes a decision by getting around their judgment: hiding facts, inventing pressure, or leaning on a bias in a way they wouldn't agree to.
Both can use emotion, stories and timing. The difference is whether the other person ends up seeing more or less.

image.label: Two paths to the same yes: one lit, one hidden
image.brief: 같은 "Yes" 문으로 가는 두 갈래 길. 왼쪽 길은 밝고 안내판(사실, 비용, 근거)이 보임. 오른쪽 길은 안개 속에 가려진 표지판과 숨은 함정. 단순한 플랫 일러스트.

cards.title: The see-through test
body: Ask: would this still work if they could see exactly what I'm doing and why? Thaler and Sunstein discuss a version of this idea in *Nudge* (2008).
A few checks make it practical:
list: **Is it true?** Real numbers, real deadlines, real scarcity
**Is it complete enough?** Nothing left out that would change their mind
**Would they choose the same with full information?**
cards.callout: If explaining your method would ruin it, it's probably manipulation.

cards.title: The technique isn't the problem.
body: A deadline is persuasion when it's real and manipulation when it's invented. Highlighting a benefit is persuasion; hiding the matching cost is not. A default option helps when most people would pick it anyway, and exploits them when it's set to profit from inattention.
So banning techniques misses the point. The same lever can inform or deceive. You judge the use, not the tool.
cards.softwareNote: This is where dark patterns live: fake countdown timers, pre-checked add-ons and cancel buttons buried five screens deep. Each one lifts a metric only because users don't notice it.

cards.title: The line is real, but blurry.
body: Good intentions don't pass the test on their own. If you're sure the hire or the product helps them, you still don't get to hide the downside.

The opposite mistake costs money too. Some people get so wary of influence that they stop making their case at all. A customer who never hears about something useful hasn't been protected. Persuading well is part of the job.

cards.title: Now it's a freight contract.
body: You sell trucking capacity to manufacturers. Your company has announced that rates rise in January. A mid-size client is deciding whether to sign a two-year contract now.

options.text: Explain the January increase, offer to lock today's rate, and point out the renewal and exit terms
options.feedback: The pressure is real and the terms are visible, so the deal holds up if they reread it later. You may lose a few who would have signed blind.

options.text: Lock today's rate, with an auto-renewal clause and 90-day notice tucked into the appendix
options.feedback: Renewals go up only because the client didn't notice. You trade a few extra months of revenue for a buyer who feels tricked.

options.text: Share a case study from your happiest client
options.feedback: Real stories are fine evidence. If that client is far from typical, say so, or the case study quietly overpromises.

cards.title: Persuade in a way that survives being seen.
body: Persuasion helps people see more. Manipulation works because they see less. The test is whether your method would still work if they watched you do it.
**Try it today:** pick one pitch, sign or offer you use. Imagine explaining exactly how it works to the customer. Does it still work?
